utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone from the Chamber as well. Mr. Josse, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, but I think I should deal with one or two preliminary matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- in relation to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because if I don't give the introduction, I know Mr. Tieger will do it for me in any event, quite understandably, let me hastily add. This witness arrived in The Hague on Monday. He brought with him quite a lot of documents. I could advance an explanation of sorts as to why they hadn't been forwarded to the Defence in advance of his coming here, but frankly, Your Honour, that explanation wouldn't be terribly satisfactory and wouldn't help the situation that the Chamber, Prosecution, and to some extent the Defence now face. He brought them, in any event. I had someone look at them, give me some assessment of them, and yesterday, after Court, so at about 6.30, I personally served them on my learned friend Mr. Tieger, in B/C/S, of course, and completely untranslated. The position is that they have now been collated and put into bundles with some sensible tabs. However, of course, they remain completely untranslated. There are quite short passages in most of the documents that I wish to use in the course of this witness's testimony, and, well, subject to the views of the Chamber, I will do my best, using the ELMO, in the course of the witness's testimony. Copies of the documents have been provided to the translation booths to try and make matters a little bit easier, although I appreciate, as I keep saying, that the situation is very far from ideal. The Prosecution are rightly concerned and upset about the situation. They've been as cooperative as they can be, but I know my learned friend wishes to make some observations to Your Honour and Your Honour's colleagues, and I well understand that, and I thought I would go first by preambling the situation and explain the dilemma that the Defence case and have imposed, I'm afraid, on everyone else in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, the French have a saying "tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner," understanding is fine, and I take it that you understood the French, but it doesn't appear on the -- it doesn't appear on the transcript. Understanding everything is -- but perhaps I have to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Understand is to forgive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- than to forgive, yes, is to forgive everything. That's, of course, not what we're heading for. I mean, the Chamber in the beginning has, well, accepted, although reluctantly, that what in my language would be called child diseases, that is, the diseases someone suffers when he is not grown up yet, in the beginning of the Defence case, but it's certainly not meant to be the beginning of a tradition. I do understand that further meetings are held on scheduling and preparing for the Defence case. I think it doesn't need any explanation to say that the Chamber becomes quite impatient and that we want the situation to change rather quickly. Mr. Tieger, is there anything you'd like to say in response to what Mr. Josse said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very little, Your Honour. I appreciate Mr. Josse's accurate explanation of the facts at the outset. So I'll just say -- mention two things quickly, one directly connected with his comments, the other related but not directly connected. First, as I foreshadowed earlier, both to the Defence and to the Chamber, under the circumstances, at a minimum, in response to this situation, the Prosecution will not be in a position to cross-examine today. We have committed ourselves to doing the best we can under the circumstances and we will endeavour to minimise the inconvenience to the Court, but I can indicate at the outset that, at a minimum, that that will be the Prosecution's position. Secondly, the related matter concerns the 65 ter summaries that have been received for witnesses who have been identified as next in order. We have been expecting for some time the more detailed 65 ter summaries. I won't go into the nature of the current summaries because I don't believe it's necessary. I think Mr. Josse acknowledges their deficiencies. But with respect to Mr. Banduka and Mr. Kasagic and a witness whom we understand the Defence will seek protective measures for, nothing has been received and I think we're already beyond the 14-day deadline, and that's a matter of growing concern to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber shares your concerns. Any other issue to be raised? If not, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. I will say a few words on another matter that was still pending as to the order of examination of a witness. The Chamber would very much follow, I would say, the lines of logic in this respect. That means examination-in-chief, a witness comes with, I would say, everything's new, the Prosecution then may cross-examine the witness, either challenging the testimony given or introducing even some new matters under Rule 89(H). The Defence then, of course, is in a position to again challenge especially what was raised in cross-examination, new issues or important new elements, new aspects. If there's no cross-examination, of course there's no need to respond in terms of questioning the witness on those matters. And therefore, also, only exceptionally there will be any need for the Prosecution to put further questions to the witness, since the Defence is expected not to raise any new issues in re-examination. But if, exceptionally, new issues or new important elements are raised, then of course the Chamber would give an opportunity to the Prosecution to put further questions to the witness. A similar system would apply if anything is raised newly by questions of the Judges. So it's mainly a matter of logic rather than to say there will never be an opportunity for the Prosecution to put further questions after the witness has been re-examined by the Defence, but it's mainly a matter of assessing what's new. If, for example, the Defence would have forgotten to put one or two questions and would do that in re-examination, then of course there would be an opportunity for the Prosecution to put further questions on that issue to the witness. Is this clear enough, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Presumably, if as a result of questions from the Bench, either party wish to ask questions arising from the Bench's questions, that is permissible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Each party can do so, and of course that even could raise some new issues or new elements. But the general logic is clear. If there's anything introduced as a new item or as a new element, the other party can ask questions in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I take it that you're Mr. Milincic. Mr. Milincic, before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Milincic. You'll first be examined by Mr. Josse, who is counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you give the Chamber your name, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Milos Milincic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, I'm going to lead you through your background, if I may. It's right that you are by profession a school teacher?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your subject was language and literature?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You taught at a school in Srbac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you were for some years a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You joined the SDS when it was founded in July of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At least a founder member, so far as Srbac was concerned, and soon thereafter became a member of the Main Board of that political party?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the multi-party elections in November 1990, you were elected to the Municipal Assembly of Srbac and then, in fact, became its president?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You held that position until 1997, when --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- your party lost the election; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For how long did you remain a member of the Main Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: For 12 years, from 1990 until 2002, 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Returning to your personal circumstances, having lost the election, you found yourself without a job in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I was not working for almost two years. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And after that two-year break you got a job in the municipality; you then went back -- I don't -- the detail of which, certainly for my purposes, doesn't matter. It's right, isn't it, you got a job in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: There was a service in the municipality that I worked for, the social welfare centre, so I did not go back to teaching, but rather to the social services of the Srbac municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You then became a teacher for a further year after that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. A year later I went back to teaching.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that leads us to 2001, where you were appointed to your present job, which is head of the pedagogical college in Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Pedagogical institute, that is, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Returning, if we may, to 1990 and the elections, how was it that you came to be president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Five parties took part in the elections, which were the first multi-party elections since 1945. Out of these five parties, which took part in the elections in the Srbac municipality, my party, the Serbian Democratic Party, won the majority of the votes. Or, to be more precise, out of 60 MPs, which is the total number of MPs in the Municipal Assembly, the SDS won 47 seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we return to tab 1 of the exhibit bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This doesn't need to be put on the ELMO. It speaks for itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is the list of parties and candidates at the election on the 5th of November of 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if we turn to list number 3, we see the Serbian Democratic Party and that you were their second candidate.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And just take us, very briefly, through the five parties. List number 1 is which party, please? If you go to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The first list is the Serbian Renewal Movement. The second list of candidates is that of the League of Communists of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Socialist Democratic Party, and Democratic Socialist Union. The third list is that of the candidates of the Serbian Democratic Party. The fourth list is that of the Party of Democratic Action. And the fifth list is that of the candidates of the Union of Reform Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, as you've already told us, you in fact were the second candidate on the SDS list. How was it that you became the president of the municipality if you were only the second candidate on your own party's list?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was not a custom for the person who is elected president of the assembly later on to be necessarily placed first on the list. My party thought that I was the more suitable person for the job, and since my party had the majority, after the elections, it was thought that the other MPs were going to vote in favour of electing me, which proved to be the case, in fact. The assembly, therefore, including the MPs of the other parties, voted for me, as an SDS candidate, in addition to the 47 SDS MPs; therefore, also the other MPs voted for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've been very helpfully advised, Your Honour, by the registrar that it's best to take a number for each -- a Defence exhibit number for each tab, as we go along. I appreciate they can't be admitted into evidence until translations are received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 1, Your Honours, will be D92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, I take it that the absence of any translation doesn't bother you that much in respect of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. That's correct, Your Honour. It doesn't present a problem with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In which case, we won't submit it. We will not submit it, Your Honour, unless Your Honour wishes us to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it is clear that it's a list of candidates -- I have some hesitation as far as especially the heading is concerned. If we would have the heading, up to the first candidate, Lela Radinkovic, perhaps that one line translated, I see that the last -- "prebivaliste" may be some kind of origin or place of birth. But if we would know that, I mean, it could be a relatively short document, leaving out all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I completely agree, and that's essentially the point I wanted to make. And perhaps it's helpful if I clarify precisely what I meant when I acknowledged that the absence of a translation at this point didn't cause particular difficulties. I simply meant that I understood the nature of the document and the witness's references to it, without the translation. Nevertheless, the translation that the Court has indicated it seeks I think is quite necessary, and we reserve any final judgement about the document until such time as it's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But to start with, then, Mr. Josse, if -- those who are going to translate it in such a way that we do not need all the names and of course it says Serbian either in -- for males or females, Serbian and then what a Yugoslav is and what a Muslim is, that should not be a problem. But all the headings of the list should be translated, as well as the, of course, the last page, date, names of those who signed it, where it comes from. But there's no need to type again the name of 180 or 200 persons. That's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've dealt with the results of the election. It's right that it's effectively an agreed fact that over 90 per cent of the population of your municipality was of Serbian ethnic origin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the result was that there were two seats won in this 1990 election, by the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to the number of votes, they got two seats in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of work within the assembly in its early days, what was the relationship like between your party, the SDS, and the two SDA members?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: It was very correct. We believed that after the fall of communism, or rather, after the first multi-party elections, it was only natural for the parties like the SDA, HDZ, and SDS to exist, and that we ought to communicate with them and develop programmes that would maintain and improve the standard of living in our municipality, in view of the circumstances. We had contacts on a regular basis, and I wish to say that on our own initiative we suggested that the vice-president of the assembly be an MP from the SDA. The assembly endorsed this motion, and Mr. Halid Haliselimovic was the vice-president of the Srbac Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before we turn to him, what was it that united your party with the SDA in those early days in your Municipal Assembly? What was the common enemy, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "Enemy" is a very strong word. We believed that communism Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. suppressed the national identities of Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, some sort of artificial approach was taken in relation to these peoples, and therefore, it was only natural for the SDA, HDZ, and SDS to democratically define their own identities, but also to compete in a normal environment for their own interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And moving back to Mr. Hadziselimovic, what were the SDS trying to demonstrate by having an SDA vice-president?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: In Srbac municipality we have a place called Kobas, where 940 Muslim families lived. It was only logical for a representative of the people, of these people, to represent the interests of the place, because he was best placed to do so and he would be more able to do so in his capacity as the vice-president. There was only one technical difficulty later, in that Mr. Hadziselimovic is a pensioner living in Zagreb, or rather, was a pensioner living in Zagreb, and voted in Kobas. Therefore, subsequently, a conflict of interest emerged that he was unable to be an MP for this particular municipality. In general, he was an open person, easy to communicate with, and a very suitable first person for dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll come back to him a little bit later, if we may. Could we turn to tab 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The way I suggest we do this is if you take the front page -- I don't think that needs to go on the ELMO. Could you simply begin by reading us the heading of this particular document, the first four words at the very -- the first four words, at the very, very top, in bold letters.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the beginning of the text pursuant to Article 304, paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to the word that begins s-l-u-z-b-e-n-i at the very, very top, the heading.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, "Official Gazette of Srbac municipality," is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is. And this is dated the 4th of January, 1991. Am I right in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The 4th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to go to the third page of this document, please, and that perhaps we should put on the ELMO. Number 6, could you read from the word spelled r-j-e-s-e-n-j-e, which I understand means "decision."

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "Decision on the election of the president and members of the regulations commission of the Srbac Municipal Assembly." Below it is stated -- or rather, we have the election of the president of the commission, Marija Krstic. She was a member of a different party. She was a high school teacher, a Croat, and she was nominated for a member of the commission, as well as the list of the MPs. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you just stop there for a moment. We see that this part of the document is heavily marked. Who has marked the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I highlighted these parts, together with others from the municipality, prior to my arrival here, in order to show that in 1991, in the municipality, we advocated the interests of all the peoples, including Croats, Serbs, and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You answered my second question. I only asked you who had marked it. You've told us why you've marked it as well. Let's move to the next list. I think we can go through these quite quickly. Number 7, please. This is another commission, isn't it? This is a commission for social monitoring; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Decision on the election of the president and members of the commission for social monitoring. Under number 4, there is Halid Hadziselimovic, therefore, the vice-president of the Srbac Municipal Assembly, a member of the SDA, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And number 8, all I think I need you to do, please, is to read where it says "listu," what this list is in relation to, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: A list of MPs taking part or witnessing matrimonies. It is stated: "The following MPs will be present at the entering into marriages on the territory of the municipality of Srbac." Furthermore, it is stated: "The territory in terms of the Registrar's Office, Bosanski Kobas, and the persons stated are Halid Hadziselimovic, Milenko Malesevic, Dr. Afif Abusafija. It's not stated here, but I know he is a medical doctor. Maid Zukanovic, Ljubomir Devic, and Boro Vucenovic. Out of the six names listed here, three are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, why was it in relation to these various lists and commission members that your party was keen to include members from other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Well, simply because, as I've indicated a while earlier, we believed that after the multi-party elections, all the peoples, therefore, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, had to be allowed to fully express themselves. It was only normal for the marriages in Kobas to be dealt with by a Muslim. It also reflected the political will of the citizens of Srbac, which was our duty, to reflect their will. It might -- you might find it confusing, the fact that etymologically, Srbac dated -- the name of Srbac dated from 1920s. Therefore, it was not a newly construed name. It dated decades back in history.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could tab 2 be given a provisional number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D93, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness now go to tab 3. I don't think the first page needs to be put on the ELMO. It speaks for itself. It's clearly the gazette for the 11th of March, 1991. The same four words. We see the date. It's the very last page, page 19, that I would like put on the ELMO, please. I'm sorry. We'll need to look at the page before to make sense of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the very bottom of page --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The penultimate page, the very bottom, show the witness that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you'd read the decision on the very bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "Decision --"

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not worried about the one at the top of that page. The bottom of the page and then turning over.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "Decision on the election of the president and the members.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Turn to the final page. Continue reading.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "The committee of the committee for religious matters." And then it goes on to say: "The committee on religious matters will consist of the following members," and five names are quoted. And one name in particular, number 5, is of interest to us here. His name is Safet Okanovic, who was a Muslim, and he is a member of that committee, the committee on religious matters. And yes, as I said, Safet Okanovic was a member of that committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what did the committee for religious matters do, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: They dealt with various issues, ranging from the construction work or restoration of religious buildings or the return of the property that may have been taken away unlawfully. They dealt with religious customs and the display of such customs. Well, that more or less sums it up, the work of the said committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D94, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to tab 4. This is the same type of document. This is the gazette for the 29th of -- I assume it's March. Could I just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In respect of tab 3, Mr. Tieger, again the question is, the Prosecution has presented at numerous occasions decisions which were part of an Official Gazette, either of a municipality or of the Republic. I wonder whether everything should be translated here. Because there's many, many pages, which may well be relevant. I do understand that context very often is an issue. At the same time, there's an opportunity to review the other decisions on the basis, I would say, on, first of all, their title. And it might well be that there seems to be totally irrelevant, whereas some other decisions, elections of, well, let's say, committees which would deal with the environment or housing or that the Prosecution would consider them to be relevant as context. But would there not be a possibility to sit together to see what the other decisions are about and whether there's any need to have them translated, or even, Mr. Josse, to agree with the Prosecution that the decisions you mentioned could be separated from the whole of the Official Gazette? Because we're now talking about the Official Gazette of the 11th of March, but of course the Prosecution could say that from a point of view of context, it should be really necessary to see the previous one and the later one as well. And then we end up in a mess of paper we never paid attention to for totally unclear reasons. So I would very much like to see whether there could be any agreement on what to translate, what to tender at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, and I think that's a practical, expedient, and I think that is in general an approach and philosophy that guided us in earlier parts of the case as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we then -- although provisional numbers are given, it might well be that they finally will be assigned to one portion only and that we receive only a translation of that portion, or that there's an agreement that only that portion should be translated. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So we're looking at tab 4, Mr. Milincic. This is the 29th of March, and it's the -- strana 10 that we need, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is decision number 12. Would you read this quite slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision on an MP's end of term in office. There are two MPs here whose term of office has ended. Number 2 is of interest here, and it says, I quote --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you to read number 1 as well, please, slowly. Read number 1 as well on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: So number 1: "It is confirmed that the term of office of Radovan Anicic, an MP of the SDS party at the Municipal Assembly of Srbac has been terminated because he has become a civil servant as of the 29th of April, 1991." Number 2: "It is hereby confirmed that the term of office of the MP of the SDA party, Abusafija, Afif has been terminated before the official end of term because he has handed in his resignation as of the 29th of April, 1991." And number 3: "This decision is to be published in the Official Gazette of the municipality of Srbac."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we see it's signed by you, as the president; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So this is one of the two SDA members resigning from the assembly. Do you know why this gentleman resigned?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Because of the conflict of interest, the first one of these two councillors referred to here has handed in his resignation. He could no longer continue to work in his current position, in his position at the time, and act as a civil servant as well. And this second councillor, Abusafija, Afif, moved to Slavonski Brod, where he found employment as a gynaecologist in Slavonski Brod, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you chose to bring this particular document with you; that's right, isn't it, Mr. Milincic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I wanted to submit this document to the Trial Chamber for the sake of the inhabitants of the municipality of Srbac who are following this trial with a great deal of attention, and their goal back then, and now, has always been to show that we never felt that the municipality of Srbac was not big enough for all ethnic groups. What I mean by this is that there was a maximum level of tolerance and that the appointment of these people, of the people from those ethnic groups, was a practical, tangible proof of that. And the events that followed confirm that our attitude was the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D95, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I just said -- this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll go straight to tab 5, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you'll touch upon the matter, Mr. Josse. Replacement of these two members of the assembly is something you'll come to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll deal with it after tab 7, when we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise I would have put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 5, similar type of document. This one's dated the 21st of May of 1991, and it's page 4 that we require, please, decision number 6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "The decision on the approval for the exchange of a plot of land, which is state property, for the plot of land for Vakuf Mosque from Bosanski Kobas." And then it goes on to say that the Islamic association Vakuf Dzamija, from Bosanski Kobas has been granted the approval to exchange the plot of land and there are references to the land register, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So, as you've just told us, the bits beneath the number 1 are the details of where exactly the land can be found; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you read, then, number 2, beginning "za," the very bottom of that first column.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: It says: "The implementation of this decision with regard to the records in the land register will be carried out by the land register of the Tribunal in Srbac and the municipal service for real estate."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Number 3.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "This decision is to be published in the Official Gazette of the municipality of Srbac," and then there is the number 04/14765 and the date, the 21st of June, 1991. And the president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, could you put that -- explain that in some other language? What does this mean? What was the municipality deciding by this particular order or decision?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I think that this committee on religious affairs came up with the initiative for a certain plot of land which belonged to the Islamic community to be exchanged for a more favourable plot which was owned by the municipality and that they could use it for certain purposes that the Islamic community felt were needed, and their plot of land was not adequate, was not acceptable. There were some problems and they tended to think that if there was this exchange of plots, they would have been able to solve their problem. And the Municipal Assembly accepted that. It was a logical thing to do because there were other instances of exchanges of plots of land. And I think that the initiative came from this committee on religious affairs, and they raised it at the assembly, or submitted it to the assembly. And this provides one practical answer as to what was normally dealt with by this committee. They made a suggestion to the assembly and then the proposal was finally carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D96, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, if you have dealt with this matter, I'd like to put some additional questions to the witness. What were the problems, and where was the one plot situated, and where was the other one situated? I mean, you said the one exchanged for more favourable to the Muslim community. For what reasons was it more favourable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it was in order to build some kind of building or whether it was to be used for a house or religious building or simply in order to use it as an agricultural field. At any rate, I don't remember. But they felt that it was better for them. And it says here what the size of the plot was as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see some square metres mentioned. But you said "they considered." That committee consisted of a large majority of Serbs and one Muslim. Was the exchange of plots of land fully supported by the Muslim community or was it only suggested by the committee on religious matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the original proposal came from the Islamic community, and that's how the whole process got started. It wasn't the other way round. First of all, they suggested it, and then it went through the committee on religious affairs, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say the exchange was fully supported by the Muslim community. Thank you for that answer. Please proceed. We still do not know exactly why it was better and you have no answer to that, but -- of course, if you don't know, you can't tell us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 7, please. I should just add, Your Honour, that the Court will observe there is no tab 6. There are a number of tabs missing. They were documents that were originally provided that we decided were superfluous. For what it's worth, the Prosecution do have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we consider that the empty second tab 4, which I find in my binder as non-existent as well. I have two tabs 4, one empty and one filled. But let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So tab 7, same, gazette, 19th of August, 1991. Could we turn, please, to the last page, page 4, decision number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again, read this slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "A decision on the end of term of office of a councillor." And then number 1: "It is confirmed that the term of office --" and there is a typing error here. It is Hadziselimovic, instead of Madziselimovic so it is an H instead of M. So, at any rate, his term of office is terminated and he's a member of the SDA party in the municipality of Srbac, and the reason for this is that he is declared that he's no longer resident on the territory of SRBH.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And can you give us any more details about that, where Mr. Hadziselimovic moved to and why?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: He moved to Zagreb. He used to work in Croatia, in Zagreb. And for a certain period of time, he came back to Kobas when he retired, and then he returned to Zagreb once again. And he cancelled his residence in Kobas and he left and went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And just read us number 2 as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "It is hereby confirmed that the term of office of the councillor, Milo Miljevic, the councillor of the SDS party in the Municipal Assembly of Srbac has been terminated because he has handed in his resignation." And number 3: "This decision must be published in the Official Gazette of the municipality of Srbac." And the date is the 19th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By the 19th of August, 1991, it means that the two SDA members of your Municipal Assembly had both resigned. Were they replaced?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The assembly wanted the next people on the list to be called, but the SDA party -- well, first of all, they came to the assembly meetings on a number of occasions. What I mean is the people who were next on the list. And then they stopped attending. And their rationale was that the quorum was there, even if they were not. So they did not put it in writing; they just said that there was no need for them to attend because there was a quorum anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how did this affect, first of all, the running of the assembly? Did it have any effect?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Purely formally speaking, no, because out of 60 councillors, well, if two, six, five, or ten are missing, you still have the required majority. But the other aspect, the political aspect, is another story altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was my next question. What effect did it have politically?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim representatives had candidates in other parties, not just in the SDA. But we wanted the SDA members to be present within the assembly at all costs, because we saw no reason whatsoever for them not to be there. And I recall a conversation with these candidates who were next on the list, and they said to me that they were farmers; they didn't have time to spare; and that Halid, since he was retired, and Dr. Afif as well, were people who could manage all that. But since they had gone, well, those two chairs would be left empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've described the political effect. Was there any effect on inter-ethnic relations as a result of there being no SDA members in your assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No. The subsequent events were to show that -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 7 will be D97, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one additional question, Mr. Milincic. Was there ever a decision which was published that next on the list had become members of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that decision here. I didn't even ask the relevant services at the municipality of Srbac for a copy. I'm not sure whether we do have that decision or not. It's my mistake that I did not look it up before coming here. In case SDA put anything in writing, we should perhaps have a copy of that, but it would have been logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not talking about logics, but I'm talking, rather, about facts, and not whether the SDA did put anything in writing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this a decision which -- usually, if a representative body is -- if the composition is changed, this is usually established formally by that body itself, so therefore, one would expect a decision here by the Municipal Assembly to say, just as the decision says, this person and that person left, who is now the member of that assembly? So I would expect, as a matter of fact, such a decision which also, by other means, could be perhaps established, such as attendance lists, where the new names appear. Because it's rather vague. You said some of the ones who were next on the list were present at some meetings and then they did not appear any more. Is there any way you could provide the Chamber with a decision that they were admitted as members of the assembly, or would there be any way of providing the Chamber with, for example, attendance lists on which these new names appear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't provide that proof because I have nothing. I would just like to add that at that time we were only learning about democracy. Now it is quite clear to all that when a name is dropped, there is a clear provision as to who should deal with replacements. But those were the first multi-party elections, and we were only beginners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get things perfectly clear. You say you can't provide that proof because you have nothing. I do understand that you haven't got such decisions brought with you to The Hague. But are you aware of whether such decisions at all exist? Because then we could look at the Official Gazette of Srbac to see whether we can find them. Do you have any knowledge on whether they exist, decisions replacing the SDA members that left by new SDA assembly members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That gives a different impression from what we heard earlier, which was a kind of a -- that there was a replacement, but it was they that finally did not show up any more because not needed for the quorum, but that you had a totally different position. I now understand that they might never have been formally admitted to be members of the assembly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they could never have exercised any voting rights if they were never formally admitted as members to the assembly, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sworn in and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That never happened, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then remind you that you're supposed to tell the whole truth, because the answers you gave suggested quite clearly that there was a replacement, but it was due to their non-appearance, that they did not participate in the work of the assembly any more. Whereas on my question now, it clearly appears that they never were admitted formally as members to the assembly because, as you said, you still had to learn about democracy, which is a quite different picture from the picture you gave us before. Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are a few things flowing from that, Mr. Milincic. Do you accept -- well, I'm going to deal with it. Do you accept what the learned Judge has just said to you? It's a statement, but let's turn it into a question. I can repeat it, if need be. He says that -- he's suggesting to you that you weren't telling the truth deliberately. Do you accept that as right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least not the whole truth. That's what I said. If that's the same to you -- I make a difference between telling a couple of things that is right. Because I can't say that they -- and I did not understand that the witness was not telling the truth, that some people appeared, perhaps, although not exercising any voting rights, but that they were in a hall where they met and they finally didn't show up any more. I'm not saying that's not the truth. Of course I have to assess. We have further to determine how credible that is. But it's certainly not the whole of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'll correct what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, do you accept that you were deliberately or otherwise not telling the whole truth a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: First of all, I said that the general public in Srbac was following my testimony here, and I had to be -- I have to be fully honest. There is something that I want to tell you. You don't have to believe me. With Sabija's [as interpreted] departure for Slavonski Brod, the SDA practically ceased to exist in Srbac, because he was the president of the party. I suppose that there was no longer a person in place to insist for the -- to new SDA councillors to be formally instated in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That, in fact, leads to my very next question, which I wanted to develop with you. Tell us, slowly and in some detail, what the constitutional position within your municipality was when a person ceased to be a member of the assembly. Let's make it simple, for one moment. Let's assume that an SDS member, the one we dealt with earlier, has become a civil servant and therefore was no longer eligible to serve on the assembly. What was the procedure, precisely, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The municipal service would ask a given party to nominate the candidate who is next on the list. As soon as the technical service of the assembly receives the nomination, the assembly proceeds to officially endorse a new councillor. I indicated that, with Abusafija's departure for Brod, the SDA lost its leadership in Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Supposing there was no nomination forthcoming from the political party. What would then happen?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I think it was logical for the technical service to deal with all the procedural matters, proprio motu, necessary for the inauguration of a new councillor, and then the rest would be within the powers of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, what in fact happened? We've heard -- you've told us that these two members of the SDA resigned for one reason or another. You've told us that after they resigned, they were not replaced by members of the SDA. Firstly, why were they not replaced by members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I don't know the reason why. I told you what I assumed, that once they were lost without their -- were left without their leadership, without the president of the party, that the party somehow became inactive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And my last question on this particular question is this: I think you mentioned earlier that their two seats remained vacant. When no one was nominated to fill their places, did another political party fill the void or did those two particular places on the assembly remain, as you've just said, vacant?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No. No other political party filled the vacant post that used to belong to the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I suppose I should ask you this: From which party did the new vice-president of the assembly come?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: We did not elect a vice-president anymore because we had wanted for the vice-president to be a representative of the Muslims. Since this was not the case, we would have had to vote for a Serb to be put on that position, and we felt that there was no need for that. We had the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would the failure of the SDA to fill their -- either of their two places be something that would need to be published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Probably it would. I'm not a lawyer, though. Formally, we do have proof of him -- of them having ceased to hold those posts, but we do not have any other decisions or anything that would have been published in the municipality's Official Gazette. The subsequent events were to take up all of our attentions, rather than the filling of the vacant posts in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still have one or more additional questions to the issue, unless you have not finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to move on to another topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You more or less blamed the fact that Mr. Hadziselimovic was not there any more; he had left for not filling in the posts. But isn't it true that Mr. Hadziselimovic only left after the -- we look at these decisions, the one about Abusafija, Afif, who, as I read it well, was a decision of late April 1991, whereas Mr. Hadziselimovic left only mid-August, so a couple of months when he was still there, and you told us that he was the president of the SDA to refill that place. And in relation to that, another question, and perhaps you can give an answer together, that you testified that they came a couple of times to the assembly meetings. Now, if they're next on the list, and if, as you said, you wanted SDA members to be present within the assembly at all costs, why not formally accept them as members? I mean, they came, you told us, a couple of times. I have some difficulties in understanding how the absence of leadership which took place only a couple of months after the first member to be replaced is to blame for it, when they appeared in that assembly but were not appointed as members. So I have some difficulties in understanding the logic of your explanation. But help me out, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Assembly sessions were held not more than once a month. It is difficult for me to say now from my memory whether these persons came once or twice to attend these sessions, and more so in the capacity of observers, in order for them to ascertain whether they were to be able at all to discharge these functions. Now, Dr. Safi [as interpreted] Hadziselimovic, as far as his relationship with the others in the party is concerned, I cannot vouch for that. I don't know how good their relations were. This was something that was taking place in Kobasi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse. But looking at the clock, I see that we are at one and a half hours. If this would be a suitable moment for you, since you were moving to your next subject anyhow, we'll have a break until ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before we move to your next subject, Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. Witness, I wish to ask you the following thing: Regarding this kind of withdrawal from the SDA -- of the SDA from political life at municipal level, could you please give me your personal explanation for it. I'm not quite satisfied when I hear you say that the two possible candidates were farmers and that they had other things to do. You are an educated man, you are a responsible man. When the events took place, you must have had some understanding of the political overall situation, over the social situation in your country, and you probably have some explanation for the fact that the SDA sort of withdrew. And I'd like to hear your personal analysis of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right in saying that they were not the only two councillors who were farmers. There were others who were farmers, too, and that is true. My explanation of their withdrawal is the following: I suppose that they were following the lines and the policies at the central level. One of the two went to Zagreb, the other one to Slavonski Brod. Then those who remained seemed not to have been able to replace them. And this was perhaps the reason why we were unable to further develop our inter-party relations. I may not be right, but I note that the president of the party left and the party itself disappeared. In the beginning, representatives of this party arrived and then later on they seemed not to arrive any longer. Perhaps it was the fault of the assembly not to have pursued the matter further to see what the reasons behind their absence were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, you know, in the life of a municipality, as such, when you have important functions, when you are responsible for the political life in such a municipality, you're bound to have conversations, exchanges, including with people, people, as it were, in the opposition. There is a Muslim minority in your municipality. Now, following the withdrawals, and when the SDA declined any participation, you did not have any conversation with some individuals from that party? That's what I'd like to understand, to hear from you. What did you hear around? What were people talking about? How did you understand the overall situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, when someone tells you that he was placed on the list of councillors, without having been consulted at all, then I wonder what's wrong. When you have a person arriving at an assembly session telling you that he was placed on the list without having been consulted first, well, what do you respond to that? How do you respond to that? They had to have six [as interpreted] names on the list. That was probably the reason. With hindsight, now, one can see the situation with more clarity. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. As I've said, those were the first multi-party elections. We were all greenhorns. I know what I would do now if I were president of the assembly. I would nominate another person. At the time, I failed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have one question, if you don't mind. In your municipality, as we know, the Muslims were really in a minority. The Serbian population was the majority population. On the other hand, you showed us -- at least Mr. Josse showed us, through the documents that were submitted to us, he showed us that your municipality, if I'm right, is a municipality where there was tolerance, where Muslims had been integrated, had been put on board in various committees, so that their community could be represented; is that right? Now, in neighbouring municipalities, what was the situation like at the time? Was there acute tension? Was there sort of violence by one ethnic group against another? How was it in your neighbours' municipalities 60 kilometres away from you? How was the situation? Could you hear on the radio or could you read in the newspapers? What were your friends telling you? What was happening, really?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be quite frank and give you a somewhat spontaneous answer. Writer Tolstoy in Anna Karenina stated that all happy families look like one another, whereas all those that are unhappy are unhappy in their own different ways. All the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina were unhappy in their own different ways. My attentions were totally devoted to Srbac municipality and the population there. And being a spontaneous, straightforward person, I had more difficulties with some Serbs who, at that point in time, thought that democracy was merely a rifle to be held in one's hand. We had murders. The family Malesevic was murdered by the Serbs. So this Serb who killed a Serbian family was convicted and then pardoned and then other families were mistreated, their fingers, ears cut off, all done by the Serbs. What I want to say is that wars are terrible evils. But I speak for my own municipality. I cannot speak for Kotor Varos, Banja Luka, Gradiska. I heard all manner of stories concerning other municipalities, some difficulties with Croats. The chief of the municipality -- of a municipality who was a Croat said that he had difficulties with the Chetniks. In the midst of all this evil, I believe that Srbac municipality managed to keep the evil at a very minor scale, and that was thanks to all the people living there, including Muslims, Croats, and ethnic Russians. Recently, the Catholic bishop Komarica, in Banja Luka, when we were inaugurating a school there, he approached me and congratulated me for the role that we had done in our municipality. I may not have given you a direct answer, but what I wanted to tell you was that I experienced and felt all that Srbac, as the municipality, was going through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just interrupt. I'm told that the witness -- it reads in the transcript "the chief of the municipality of a municipality who was a Croat said he had difficulty with Chetniks." I think it should say that he was cooperating with Chetniks. Perhaps we could just ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There might be some problem in translation. Our text reads that "The chief of the municipality -- of a municipality who was a Croat said that he had difficulties with the Chetniks." Is that what you said or did you say something different from that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. His neighbours in Novi Gradiska and Brod - these are Croat municipalities - he was criticised for being in touch with me, and he was called a Chetnik, whereas I was called an Ustasha, because we were communicating with each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That having been clarified: You told us that you didn't know what to say to someone who said that he was put on the list without even having any knowledge of it, and you said they had to put six names on that list. We just have looked at the list of the candidates. I noticed that there are 60 names --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 60 names. 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 60 names. Now I do understand. Because it was translated, I think, as -- yes. They had to have six names on the list was -- so thank you very much for that clarification, which seems to be perhaps a translation mistake. Because now it becomes fully clear to me. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In many ways, Mr. Milincic, the question I want to ask you next flows, really, from what the learned Judge, Judge Hanoteau, has just asked you. Some time ago, I asked you about the political effect on inter-ethnic relations as a result of there being no SDA members in your assembly, and you said that there wasn't any political effects, and you went on to say "the subsequent events were to show that." What subsequent events were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the war, which unfortunately developed and spilt over from Croatia to Bosnia, and our intention was to reduce the evil to the greatest extent. My municipality, Srbac, by a combination of circumstances - you have to know that Croatia's border is 50 kilometres away from us and we are separated by the Sava River. We have 22.000 inhabitants - was a pretty wealthy area. I have to tell you that we cover an area of some two -- 500 square kilometres, with some 38 inhabited places. We have large farms, although we have some problems now with the avian flu. We have a lot of livestock. And it all had to be maintained and protected, in order for us to have a constant supply of food. Because everything was at a standstill. There was no electricity, no fuel. We focussed all our efforts to deal the with profiteers who are not concerned with one's ethnicity, whether one is a Croat or a Muslim, but rather dealing in their own affairs. We tried to maintain order and good neighbourly and inter-ethnic relations. We were lucky enough to survive all that, to be -- to have been part of the Srbobran municipality during the war and after the war was a privilege. Whenever we are in Sarajevo, in the company of others, they know very well where we come from. It was in such war circumstances that we had to live and make sure that the war was kept outside our boundaries, that the schools continued working. In Kobas, we asked the chief of the police there to establish a territorial police station, a substation, that was to take care of the situation over there. These were the events that followed later on. By a combination of circumstances, Srbac survived as a municipality. I'm simply telling you the truth, how we had experienced all these events. I believe that my only satisfaction and those who will criticise me and under whose scrutiny I am are the representatives and members of my municipality, who will be following what I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was a crisis staff formed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: At some point in 1992, we received an order from AR Krajina, and AR Krajina, once again, was an institution referring to the Krajina municipalities gravitating around Banja Luka. Banja Luka was the centre. And they suggested to us, ordered us, basically, to set up a crisis staff, which would see to it that life in the municipality could function as normally as possible. In other words, they were there to prevent conflicts and to ensure proper livelihood for all our inhabitants and to provide protection from everything that comes with a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was the relationship of the Crisis Staff with the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff met almost on a daily basis, in the mornings and in the afternoons, and they analysed daily events. And the assembly would check the decisions of the Crisis Staff on a monthly basis, or sometimes they would tell them that they were unable to actually make certain decisions, with regard to consumption, mostly, or expenditure, in general. And they would tell them that in case such a decision was repeated, it would not be approved by the assembly. And so the person signing such decisions would be held accountable. So the Crisis Staff met on a daily basis, and afterwards the decisions made by the Crisis Staff would be given the assembly's blessing, whenever the assembly met, on a monthly basis, depending on the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And for how long did the Crisis Staff last?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but from 1992 up until almost 1995, thereabouts. I can't tell you exactly, but it did exist for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to look, please, at tab 8, which is another gazette, this time dated the 11th of September, 1992. Could we go to page 2, please. It's number 4, middle of the second column. Could you tell us what -- read out, actually, what that is.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Do you mean Article 4, on page 2? "With reference to Article 8--" well, it is about the fund and the board of -- for the director? Is that what you mean? In that case, you have to help me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The part that is marked, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I see. "On the basis of Article 89 of the law on regular tribunals and article 62 of the statute of the municipality of Srbac, see the Official Gazette of the municipality of Srbac number 2/92. The Municipal Assembly of Srbac, at a meeting held on the 11th of September, 1992, reached the following decision: On the appointment of the trial judges and the trial judges for minor offenders --" and actually it's for judge jurors. And there is a list of a number of names, and one name is underscored. It's number 19. The name is Senad Sejfulan, and he was appointed as a juror judge for underage offenders. And further down it says: "This decision must be published in the Official Gazette of the municipality of Srbac," and dated the 11th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what nationality -- what ethnicity was Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Senad Sejfulan is a Muslim. He was a member of the police force in the Republic of Srpska. I think he's living abroad at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And number 4 in this list of 30 names, that reads Nukic Nadir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nadir Nukic is a Muslim. He's still living in Kobas today. He is a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And summarise what these people, these 30 people who had been nominated, were meant to do. What was their role in the judicial system?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Well, apart from the president of the tribunal, they were judge jurors. I suppose that's enough. I don't know what else to say. I suppose you know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that these were not lawyers but laymen who participated in the administration of justice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think in English we'd probably call them magistrates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did they --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In England. I'm sorry, Your Honour. In England, we'd call them magistrates, rather than in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in England, also the term "jurors," which of course is something quite different in England. So let's try to -- Were they sitting alone as judges, as - Mr. Josse, correct me if I'm wrong - as magistrates are doing in England, in magistrates court, were they sitting alone passing judgements in minor cases or were they assisting or sitting in the presence of a professional judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were helping the judge and listening to what was being said. Perhaps occasionally they did say something. But they were not judges, in fact. They were members of the jury. Senad finished grammar school and he certainly wasn't a lawyer. He was a police officer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters believe it's the jury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How many would be there in a court, which was, as I understand, presided over by a professional judge? How many of these lay participants would be present in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You made a comparison, but it comes down more, I would say, to the German system, where lay participants are sitting together with one or more professional judges and that's, of course, still something unclear whether they take a judicial role, but let's not explore that in full detail. They were involved in the administration of justice. That's the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For what it's worth, Your Honour, one tier in the English system, exactly that exists, a judge sitting with two lay people on one tier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not really a magistrates court, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why were these two Muslim people nominated to sit in these courts?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, Muslims were sometimes brought to trial as well, and it was only logical that in a multinational context there would be a Muslim representative as well. Whenever there was a dispute or a case involving Muslims, those people would be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How, in your estimation, did Srbac avoid getting dragged into the Croatian war, bearing in mind it bordered the river Sava?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: This is not a place for a display of emotions, but even now I'm scared of history, of the past events, that is. I must thank the citizens of Srbac, as well as the citizens of the neighbouring Croatian town, Davor, because a great deal of pressure was brought to bear upon us on both sides for these two towns, neighbouring towns, one Serb, another Croat, to start fighting. The mayor of Davor, in Croatia, was very often criticised for the fact that he was supposedly cooperating with the Chetniks, that is to say, for us. And the same for me. I was being criticised for doing deals with the Croats. But we had very risky contacts, in fact, risky for both of us, that is, the two mayors. We would come to the river Sava in the evening and call out to one another and discuss matters which were of importance to both sides. And we very often met. We crossed over by boat. Either he came to see me or I went to see him. And snipers would be out to get us, both of us, as we were rowing across the river. And we vowed we would do everything in order to make sure that the undisputed territory, because even in World War II, there was never any problem there. There were Croats on one side, Serbs on the other side. Why would we fight? But unfortunately, I must state that there was a great deal of envy on both sides and there were forces trying to push us into conflict. And it was probably the only municipality that never entered the fray, as it were, and we're all proud of it. Both the Serb and the Croat press talked of us in a certain way. Bishop Komarica, for the second time, praised the citizens of Srbac for what they did and the way they conducted themselves in preventing a war and in making sure that no dispute arose from a situation where there was no problem. And many students from Croatia came to the school in Srbac. They attended our school and I was their teacher. So all that, in a way, at a certain point, when things got difficult, made it kind of easier for us to -- not to rush into anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps tab 8 should be given a number, Your Honour, before I turn to tab 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D98, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 10, could I comment to the Court by saying this: It is the most unwieldy by far, and I'll try and deal with it in summary, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This collection of documents show what, please, Mr. Milincic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: These are decisions on the basis of which former members of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Srpska, those members who were Muslim, that is, are granted invalidity rights or pensions. Let me just point out that in the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska, there were 89 Muslims and 66 others, such as Ruthenians, Czechs, Ukrainians, Croats. Unfortunately, three Muslims were killed. And these people here had been wounded and they were recognised as having been disabled between 50 and 100 per cent, and these are papers stating that they would be granted their invalidity rights or benefits.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could deal with it like this. If we look at the first document - listen carefully to my questions, please, Mr. Milincic - am I right that these are decisions of the Municipal Assembly of Srbac, department of general administration?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see the first one that you produced is in fact a recent one, 27th of April of this year.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: You know, these invalidity papers get revised on a regular basis. Some categories develop in one way, and others in another way. That is to say, some people get better; others get worse. And so this is a document dated 2005. They were assessed by this relevant committee, and this is the last instance, the last decision about that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And this relates to an individual called Sejad Djuheric; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see him on the list. So he's a war invalid, the sixth category, 60 per cent invalidity. And it goes on to say: "Continues to recognise," which means continues since the time of the war, when he was wounded. So, "continues to be recognised as a war invalid, sixth category, and 60 per cent disability, on the basis of a wound incurred in the line of duty as a member of the armed forces of the Republic of Srpska." And then it goes on to say how much money he's entitled to, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to go through these quickly, and in order. If we go to the second document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps first -- could I ask one additional question? Does it say anywhere when this person was injured, an injury which caused the decision to be taken that he should be -- that he should receive an invalidity pension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the second paragraph of the decision, it says: "This decision replaces the decision number 022560442, dated the 13th of November, 2002." So that gives us an indication there's no further detail, but any other details would be in the personal file, individual personal file. But we can see that the previous decision was dated 2002. And then in that decision, there is probably reference back to another one, and so on and so forth. I don't know. There is no indication of where or how the person was wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know the individual mentioned in this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know him. I know some others, but I don't know him. I know, for example -- I'm going to try and find one of my former students here. Mr. Kolaric.
