He's completely disabled, 100 per cent. I can't find the papers here. I know he was an outstanding student, a great mathematician. Unfortunately, he was badly wounded, but he managed to survive. Kolaric. I can't find --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it's 11th of February, 2005, is the most recent date, bears the number 02/2-560-26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I take it that you understand what I'm seeking to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to be able to help a little bit in that regard in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be great. That would be great. I've got in front of me now number 26, handwritten 26 at the top, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. There's a number that's been added in, handwritten 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the eighth copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. That's Abraham Kolaric.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we -- I was going to go through all these names, but perhaps I won't do that. Could we go to fourth from the end, please. It's a different type of form, which is in Latin, rather than Cyrillic, script.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you want to go to the sixth from the end, Mr. Josse? I've got 5 still following in Cyrillic when I start the Latin. It's about "Baranjecki, Mitar." Is that the one you had in mind or do you have a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I must have a different order, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have got only one not in Cyrillic, and that is a -- let me just check whether that's correct. Yes. I've got only one not in Cyrillic, which is the name Baranjecki, Mitar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're going to provide Your Honour with another copy. I'm sorry about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Baranjecki, Mitar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have three different names because I've now got Zukanovic, Redzo, and that's the one -- the binders aren't exactly the same, Mr. Josse. It would be preferable to receive all the same documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It certainly would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now -- from Zukanovic, Redzo in front of me, and I -- two of the Judges had -- yes. Coming close to it. Now all three Judges have Zukanovic, Redzo in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: First of all, do you know Mr. Zukanovic? Do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No. He probably knows me, and I don't know him. I know Kolaric because he was a student of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Second question is: Can you help us with his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thirdly, if we look about halfway down this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we talking about Kolaric or are we talking about -- because the witness says he doesn't know him, but -- Are you talking now about Mr. Zukanovic or are you talking about another person? When you said "he's a Muslim," who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me whether I know these people. Was that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked whether you knew a certain Mr. Zukanovic. You said that you did not know him personally. And then you continued telling us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zukanovic, no, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you know what his ethnicity is,, even if you do not know someone personally, then you might know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The name tells you what ethnicity a person is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Zukanovic, then, would be --?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What is his --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Looking at this document, about halfway down the page we see a word, and I will spell it o-b-r-a-z-l-o-z-e-n-j-e. Read that word out, please, and read the following paragraph out.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: It says: "Statement of reasons. Redzo Zukanovic, from Kobas, submitted an application to the secretariat on the 21st of December, 1999, for the recognition of his entitlement to a disability benefit, on the basis of the wound incurred in the course of his military service in the armed conflicts in --" and here it is stated, "the wounding on the 3rd of January, 1993, Grebnica village, Samac municipality, as a member of the Army of Republika Srpska." It goes on to say that he attached the requisite documentation and handed it over to a medical commission. The commission issued its own findings and opinion. Number 3518, dated 27 December 1999, wherein it established that the named person is an invalid of the sixth category, with a 60 per cent disability, valid for a period of two years. The monthly disability benefit amounts to 18 per cent of a base, and so on and so forth, in accordance with Article this and that of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see, can't we, that that decision or document is dated the 28th of December of 1999? At the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And let's look, please, briefly as well, at the other document that's in Latin script, that's dated the 18th of May of the year 2000, that relates to Mr. Berinzevski [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know him? What's his ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Ivan Berezovski was a student of mine as well, or rather, his father is a colleague of mine. He's a teacher as well. Ivan Berezovski is a member of the Ruthenians. So it's easy to identify persons by their name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think you may be looking at a different document. You are. The one you're looking at is -- I think must be in --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I have here in front of me Mitar Baranjecki. Is that what you're referring to, in Latin script.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exactly. Let's deal with that one. Do you know Mitar Baranjecki?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell from the name what the ethnicity of Mr. Baranjecki is?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Either a Ruthenian or a Czech. I don't know. He's not a Serb, Croat, or Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And just this: I just want you to read the one paragraph that begins -- just after the middle of the page, Baranjecki, Mitar 8th of March, 1998. Just read out that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "The above named person hails from Cukalo [phoen], is a war invalid of the ninth category, with 30 per cent disability, based on his wounding on the 3rd of June, 1994, at Srbobran." That's Donji or Gornji Vakuf today, I'm not sure which of these. One of the Vakufs, anyway. And then the customary lines as to what his entitlements are, that the medical commission has established that he is entitled to an invalidity benefit permanently, but for a fixed period.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. And it says, I'm sure I can lead on this, that he was a member of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In the line of duty, as a member of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could these documents, tab 10, be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 10 would be D99, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it would have each individual document, because there is some confusion about it. We should, I think, give them the numbers as they appear on the top, and that would then be A to V, including V. Yes. Could I ask one question? Have you dealt with the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us: These documents, were you in any way involved in the decisions taken on these injured persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. These were Republican commissions who handle these matters, and I have no contacts with them whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you brought the documents, so I don't know where you got them or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't bring them. No. I didn't myself. There is a municipal commission there that dealt with these matters. I left politics a long time ago. These are ongoing procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did you bring these copies of decisions to The Hague? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Three days ago I went to the municipality and asked the current mayor to provide me with the papers that I thought were relevant, and they did. It is no secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any Serbs in these documents on invalidity pensions, or are these all Muslims or Russians or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intention was the following one: Since the Army of Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking whether there are any Serbs in it. What your intention was, perhaps Mr. Josse would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but I only brought the decisions relating to the non-Serbs, as it were. But there were, of course, Serbs in the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it looks as if the applications were made, from what we have seen, and of course we were not able to study them all in sufficient detail, it seems that most of the applications were made quite a long time after the injuries took place. Is that similar for Serbs who were injured? Did they apply for pensions in the late 1990s, and no one got any invalidity pension in the mid-1990s, just after the conflict, 1996, 1997? Because I do understand -- Mr. Josse, I'm just giving you -- it seems that these documents would support the active serving in the VRS by non-Serbs, including Muslims. I see that some of the names are related to the place which we have seen very often in this municipality, if we were talking about Muslims. And on the other hand, we can't compare it with how the Serbs were treated in this respect. So therefore, it's -- the documents may have relevance in several respects, whereas we can find only on one item a clear indication. But let's leave it. If they're not there, we can't -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Josse. This does not interfere with your plan in any way. I would just like to clarify one thing. These Muslim men, or anyway, men from other ethnic groups, these people receiving these benefits, were they originally resident in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What corps of the army did they belong to? What corps were they a part of? They were wounded as soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were members -- or rather, the Srbac municipality had its own brigade deployed in various parts of Republika Srpska, and probably in some of the earlier documentation it is stated where he was wounded. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So my question is this: Do we know where all these people were wounded, in what sort of battle did they take part, on the basis of the papers that you've submitted to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that it was necessary to bring such papers. I can send a fax to the municipality asking them to send us such documents tomorrow. Of course they have to know the place where the wounds were incurred. The commission cannot decide without such papers, especially with such great requirements placed on the budget. They have to have such documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying I would like to see these papers. I would just simply like to know whether, on the basis of the existing documentation, it is possible to find out where exactly these people were wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on the basis of documentation that the commission issues decisions, and I mean the medical commission. There has to be proof of his having been wounded in the battlefield rather than in a traffic accident. This is a very serious type of decision. There can be no meddling with it. These are municipality stamps. I received these papers from official bodies. Yes, we can obtain these documents, but it may take some time. I am certain that these are truthful decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps one small additional question. Do you know whether any of them was wounded in your municipality or that they were wounded elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you any figures in terms of percentages, but I believe that most of them were wounded outside the Srbac municipality, depending on the period of time and where the brigade forces were deployed in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a bit lost, because my list is not exactly the same as yours. But we'll try to sort it out. Judge Canivell has one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I would like to be -- to get clarified one point. It seems that it's common for all those people, in spite of their ethnicity, that they were members of the Srpska Republic army. Is that the case, or is it that afterwards even people from other armies -- not exactly from the Srpska Republic, were considered also being members of this army? That means after the war it has been only one army that encompassed both the previous members of the Srpska Republica army and the people that had been Serbian in army originally from the Srpska Republic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- do I understand Your Honour's question to be did all these people serve in the VRS? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the question, Mr. Milincic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Now they are forming only one kind of army, an army which is common for ... Are they now -- why is the fact that all of them were members of the Srpska Republic army? It is because they were fighting on the side of the Srpska Republic army? No. Well, can you explain me why they are considered to be members of this army, in spite of the fact that they didn't fight during the war on the Srpska Republic side? Is it clear to you, my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to try and answer, and then you'll be able to see whether I've guessed what your question was. So all these people who are on this list, as well as a whole lot of others whose documents I didn't bring along and are of Serb ethnicity, were members of the RS army, on the basis of the fact that they were mobilised, according to the usual regulations, whatever. After the end of the war, they were all demobilised, but the wounds that they had sustained meant that they would get disability benefits, as established on the basis of their medical assessment. So they were members of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Srpska. As such, they were wounded in different battlefields, and this all -- the other Serbs or Croats, as they may be, whoever was wounded qualified for these disability benefits and these benefits are checked on a regular basis. I don't know whether I've guessed right what your question was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I would like to, if I can understand, that those people that were mobilised and were incorporated to the Srpska Republic army, even if they were Muslims. Because you had mentioned that four of them were Muslims. Were they fighting in the Srpska Republic army against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 86 Muslims were members of the Srbac Brigade, or rather - sorry - I can't remember correctly. It was 79. 79 Muslims -- I mean, I prepared for this, so I looked up all this information. So there were 79 Muslims who were within the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska and within the Srbac Brigade. There were 66 Ruthenians, Czechs, Ukrainians, and Croats, put together. And yes, they were on the front lines, so they had conflicts and engaged in battle against the Muslim and the Croat side, paradoxically speaking, but yes, there were the opposite cases. In some instances Serbs were mobilised into the BH army or the Croat army. Unfortunately, that's what civil war brings about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Did you know of some other people that didn't serve in the Srpska Republic army, at least that they were fighting in the opposite army, and if they had got wounded or injured and had become -- have got some incapacity, if they had got also this kind of pensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are civilian victims of war, people who stepped on mines or when they work in the fields or minding their cattle. Civilian victims do not fall into the same category, and are not treated in the same way as the war veterans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I do not mean only civilians. I mean soldiers included in the Srpska Republic army, they had got also incapacity pensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean they served in another army? Is that what you mean? I mean, unless they were in the armed forces of the Republika Srpska, they can't get these benefits from the Republika Srpska. If they didn't serve in the Federation Armed Forces, they can't get the rights acknowledged in the Federation. So it works both ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I'm not meaning that they are paid the pensions by the Republika Srpska person -- could be the case that they are paid by other organs. You don't know anything about those possibly wounded people, being incapable, being paid by part of the confederation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they settled in the territory of the Republic of Srpska now, they will still have the previously acquired rights, pension rights, disability benefits, whatever. Otherwise, those that -- veteran bonuses can only be paid to war veterans. They can be qualified for other types of benefits, such as people who became disabled as a result of accidents at work or whatever. We have other bodies who deal with this. Or services who help the poor, in general, disabled in general, or whatever. I really don't know if I'm getting your drift, but that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: What I wanted to know is about soldiers that haven't been fighting inside their organisation, inside the Republika Srpska army, if they had got in case they had been incapacitated, if they are getting pensions because of their wounds in the previous war. You don't know, or do you know? In case you know, why is it you haven't included anyone here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean people from World War II? War veterans still surviving from World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see if there's any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: The confusion is I'm not speaking about World War II. This is not what we are interested. I am speaking about the Bosnian war that took place in 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just seek to clarify. You are asking about soldiers receiving pensions, soldiers that -- well, let's give an example. Are you talking about Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about people that were included in the army, that was in the VRS army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: -- who had been injured and got some limitation, if they are getting pensions or not. And I had asked him about that. He says that he speaks about civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the police. If there were police officers, they would qualify. But they can't be wounded as a member of the Federation Armed Forces and get benefits from the Serb Republic Armed Forces. But if they were in Banja Luka or somewhere else, yes. But here we're talking only about people who were members of the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska, whatever their ethnicity, Ruthenian, Czech, whatever. And there were no other armed for his. There were no paramilitaries, whatever. There was just the Republika Srpska and the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau will have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like an extra clarification as well, sir. You had told us that in this brigade from your municipality, there were about 80 Muslims. Now, were those Muslims mobilised by the state authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody got an invitation to join, no matter what ethnicity they were. If they were born in a certain year, they would get that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that all Muslims who were of age would receive such an order for mobilisation from your municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All able-bodied men received such invitations and were asked to join either the armed forces or do the so-called work duty. Some expressed a wish to join the armed forces, and others wanted to provide logistical support, work as cooks or, I don't know, chop wood or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we say that all Muslims of age in your municipality were actually asked to join the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clearly stated up until what age people could be drafted, but younger lads were taken for the brigade, and all the others, the elderly men, were asked to do other things. They would watch things along the river --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please answer my question. Now, these men who had been drafted, who had been invited to join the army, did they all obey or were there any deserters, as it were? Could you answer that? Did they all join or did some of them refuse to join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very difficult to give you percentages, but the military police had their hands full as well. What does it mean? Yes, some people were taken in, I mean, Serbs, for the most part. Because there were mostly Serbs in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please answer my question. I'm referring to Muslim men now. Now, did all Muslims who were asked to join the army follow that call, or was there a certain percentage of Muslims who refused to join and who fled, who deserted the area and left and went to live elsewhere? You must know that, because you were in charge of the municipality at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Those who left, yes. Those who left are no longer there, and those who stayed behaved in line with the overall spirit within the municipality. And, I mean, it's quite another matter that some people felt, okay, if I have my wife and child who are left on their own, I can't do that. And some people are -- were allowed to go back to their homes, because otherwise there would be no livelihood for their families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, you do see the essence of my questions. Now, the Muslims who were drafted in the army, did they actually refuse to take up arms? Did they refuse on the grounds that they knew that they would be fighting against the people of their own ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any information of that, and I don't have any information of them killing people of their own ethnicity. I'm not a military person myself, and there was a military command. But as to me receiving any information of them fleeing or being deserters, I have no information about that. I do have information that there were 79 Muslims in the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska. As to how many deserters there were, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is 79, then. These 79 Muslims are how many in terms of percentages, with regard to the overall number of able-bodied Muslim men living in the municipality? Does this mean that these are all the Muslims who could have joined the army, or is it just a proportion of that population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were 940 families, so it is a proportion. And somebody did some sums and tried to calculate how many able-bodied men would there be in those families. And secondly, how many of those people would be the only providers and would have to take care of the rest of their family. And then you can calculate that. But I didn't prepare for this sort of mathematical analysis. But I could have done, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.text: Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, having said I wasn't going to return to the subject that the witness was just giving evidence about, I've been asked to ask one or two more questions, which I'm happy to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Milincic, the non-Serbs who were mobilised into the Srbac Brigade, was any pressure brought to bear upon them to join the Srbac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Frankly, nobody readily goes into the army, be it Serbs, Muslims, or Croats. But that was the period that called for such sacrifices, and people responded to the call-ups. Forcibly, what does it mean? If you refuse to respond to such a call-up, be it a Serb or a Muslim, there will be a military police coming to get you, and there were no exceptions there. And I mean exceptions in terms of responding to military call-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was the effect of the military police coming to get one? What would happen to someone who found the military police knocking on their door?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Well, that person would collect his belongings and go to his assigned unit. Sometimes they would tell the military police that they were able to go on their own, and they would then eventually go on their own to join their unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I would have one question. I hope you do not mind. To get a proper idea of what actually, in numbers, was the case, you said that there were 940 families, I do understand, Muslim families. Did you mean families or did you mean Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I meant families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That doesn't -- that does not entirely fit into the data we have got in, I think it was P954, but the big bundle of data gives a number of 940, but that's persons, not families. So we have to see -- you say there were 940 Muslim families in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see a problem there. There were 940 Muslim families, 145 Croat families. I was merely using --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpret didn't hear what the witness was using to draw upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Repeat what you've just said, please, Mr. Milincic. You said: "I don't see a problem there. There were 940 Muslim families, 145 Croat families. I was merely using --" You said something else, which the interpreter didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. 945 or 950 - I'm not certain about the figures - Muslim families; 145 Croat families in Srbac municipality. These are 1991 data. Of course, we have different data from 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am looking at the 1991 data, which - of course, we have no translation yet - would give 140 Croats, 940 Muslims, 19.380 Serbs. Is that families or is that Serb individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to the population of Srbac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have a total number of what I understand a little bit over 21.000, almost 22.000, as the total population. Yes. Then there is at least, unless, of course, we have always the problem of -- well, the problem, at least we never know exactly who called themselves Yugoslavs. Because on 940 Muslims, 140 Croats -- it seems that these numbers reflect the numbers of individuals. We also have 811 Yugoslavs, for example, which of course could disturb our view on the matter. We'll have a look at it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's move on to a completely different topic, if we may. Tab 12, please. This relates, doesn't it, to the murder of Mr. Hadziselimovic, whom you had told us had for a time being been the vice-president of the municipality. He had then, you've told us, resigned his seat within the assembly, and I think you told us he went to live elsewhere. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, let's not look at the first page, because I don't think that helps. The second page, which is the certificate with the Latin script, which is a document dated the 25th of March, 1996. Help us, please. Top left-hand corner it says "Vojni sud u Banja Luci." Read that, please, top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "Military court in Banja Luka, IK number 23/92, dated 25th of March, 1996."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We see then the name, Stanica. Continue reading it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. "Public security station Srbac. The following information is hereby being delivered for the following convicted person, first and last names, Ljubomir Stankovic, father's name, Veljko, mother's name, Koviljka, maiden name, Sancanin, born on the 30th of August, 1960, place of birth, Saferovci village, Srbac municipality, Socialist Republic Srpska, resident at Saferovci village, Srbac municipality, Republika Srpska; ethnicity, Serb; citizenship, Republika Srpska, private by occupation worker. Date and number of judgement, 20th of March, 1995, IK number 23/92. The judgement handed down by the military court in Banja Luka, for which offence," it goes on to say, "murder, under Article 26, paragraph 2, item 6, and the criminal offence of causing general danger under Article 172, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska. Sentence: Nine years of imprisonment. President of the Chamber, Captain First Class, Svetozar Davidovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How do we know which murder this refers to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I asked to be sent -- I asked for it yesterday. I know who was murdered, but you don't, and of course I will not give a false statement. I know that it incurs responsibility. You can later on verify my testimony. An offence can be interpreted in different ways. The vice-president of the municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry. You're about to tell us. Just tell us who it is and how you know. Just tell us who it is that this individual murdered, and how you know who -- who it is.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Ljubomir Stankovic mentioned herein, shot the former councillor and vice-president of the assembly, Halid Hadziselimovic, who died several days later in the hospital as a result of his wounds. You know that the president of the assembly is briefed daily, every morning, on the events for the previous 24 hours. That morning I received a written report that the evening before, in Kobas, in a cafe, and there was a name of the cafe as well, there was a fight between Ljubomir Stankovic and Halid Hadziselimovic, where Stankovic opened fire from a weapon, who was seriously wounded, taken to the hospital, and died several days later. This is the judgement handed down in relation to the same man, Stankovic, for that particular murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think, if we turn to the next document, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before we continue, exactly relevance? What is it? Is it that people were prosecuted if they would kill Muslims or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd like to deal with it very, very shortly. I mean, the main point I'd like to establish is the fact that the witness - excuse me for commenting here, but Your Honour has asked me - has made a conscious decision to bring this evidence and put it before the court. In other words, he's not trying to hide what happened to this unfortunate individual. That's really the point that I wish to establish. That's why I'm adducing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We do understand that he doesn't want to hide that this person was killed. I don't know whether we need a follow-up for this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We don't. The other two -- the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness would know anything more about how it happened, then we might be interested to know that, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm probably prepared to release the other two documents -- remove them from the bundle. Could I say, the first one in fact is simply a release document, some sort of parole-type document, and the third one relates to the man's incarceration in Banja Luka. They don't take the matter any further at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only matter we'd like to know is -- first of all, we appreciate that the witness doesn't want to hide any such events. Do you have any knowledge on what caused the fight to happen in that cafe or bar, I think you said it was? Was it just ... Hear anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I heard about this, my immediate reaction was that this was not going to be good, because immediately it was going to be interpreted as a Serb killing a Muslim. But as far as I could hear about this man, he was prone to these fights. And then I called the chief of police, asking him to conduct an investigation into this matter. This was a man who was a councillor, a former vice-president of the assembly, who lived in Zagreb at the time but came back to his weekend cottage and got killed. I felt this moral obligation toward him. He was a man who I cooperated with and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Do you know why and how that fight started? Did they find out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief of police informed me about the way things happened, and I'm telling you this now. I wasn't there. It was Bajram. He came to his village to celebrate this with his family. He was passing by a cafe there from where loud music could be heard. He entered the cafe and drew their attention to the fact that there was Bajram and that this was not proper. And what followed was a tussle. They punched each other. This man was younger. Obviously, he had a weapon with him. The man was taken to the hospital in Banja Luka, which is quite far away. There are some 70 kilometres to Banja Luka. And some two or three days later, he died. I phoned the hospital, inquiring after him, and they told me that he was in critical condition. And this is the truth of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You thank you for giving this information. Please continue, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's go to -- Could that be given a number, please? I'm happy to submit only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Only the second document. The other two can come out of the -- can come out of Your Honour's bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D100, Your Honours, dated 25th March 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we take out the others. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 13, please, Mr. Milincic. Have the tab in front of you, but it might be best if you first deal with this by narrative. As we can see from the index, these are documents relating to the destruction of the mosque in Kobas; is that correct? It's my fault. Don't worry about the documents for the moment. Put them down. Put the documents down for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us the date that the mosque in Kobas was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the paper. But from memory -- although I can't really tell you. I'm trying to find it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is it item number 5, in the -- in the document that's got 5 entries in Latin script, I think, is it the last entry from someone called Dragan?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So the 11th of July, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Your Honours have got that document, since the witness has got it, perhaps I'll deal with it a different way, using the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Read, please, as best you can, Mr. Lazarevic's entry, so in other words, beginning "Radeci," r-a-d-e-c-i.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: "On the 11th of July, 1993, at 2200 hours, Dragan Lazarevic submits this report and indicates as follows: Whilst on duty at the checkpoint in Kobas," which means that he was out in the street, "he noticed twinkling, some lights, in the direction of the mosque."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say "which means that he was out in the street," is that the literal text or do you add that to the portion you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was merely clarifying what the checkpoint meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to read, and nothing else, at this moment. Could you please restart after the word "Lazarevic, Dragan."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Whilst on duty at the checkpoint in Kobas, he noticed twinkling in the direction of the mosque. As he went over to check what was going on, he saw fire had already caught the interior of the mosque." Yes, that's right. It's not "he saw," but rather fire had already caught the interior of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Dragan Lazarevic is a police officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we see a stamp in the right-hand column. That's a police stamp, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that column, which is column 10, am I right in saying -- which begins with the word "prezime," am I right that that means the person who committed crime? So column 10 relates to person who committed crime?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Column 10 -- oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Go to the top of that -- go to --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's fine. This is where the name of the perpetrator should be indicated, and in the place where the stamp is, the word "NN," unidentified, is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's just turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before we do so, could the witness tell us what this exactly is? Is this a register of a police station or is it a -- is that a local police station? If it is, could you please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the police report concerning the events for the past 24 hours in the municipality, and what it deals with here is the fire on the mosque, or rather, in the mosque, and a police officer's report about what he had seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did you get this document from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I knew that this was going to be an inevitable topic here, I requested the police to provide me with this, because it was evident that this had happened, and although there were speculations about it, I wanted the exact information from the police as to how these matters happened. I went over, asked them to give me the papers that would indicate that this indeed had transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'll tell you what my problem is, and I hope that you'll be able to clarify. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is a 24-hours report, then not the first entry is somewhere the end of June, with the specific time, the next one is -- well, the third one is the 3rd of July. So these are not 24-hours reports. And if you look at the -- what I understand perhaps to be the location, then it's very much one village rather than -- I only see Kobas, Kobas, Kobas, Kobas. I wonder if this represents certain events. I hardly can imagine that it would present 24-hours reports. So if you would please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I, of course, don't want to give evidence, but can I help to this extent: If we look at how I hope Your Honour's bundles are created, there are two documents in the form of some sort of register. If the Court looks at the very bottom of -- in fact, the first page, the one that the witness has been reading from, the Court will see a faxed date, dated today, 09/11/05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That has been sent to the witness today, at the request of the Defence. The witness -- as has the next document, which is, I think, part and parcel of the same document. The remaining five pages in tab 13 -- which the Court is going to be relieved to hear -- are going to be, of course, later removed shortly -- the witness brought with him in order, again, to tell the Court about the destruction of this mosque. It became apparent when we talked to him that that -- those documents didn't clarify the situation sufficiently, so he made a telephone call, exactly what that call is Your Honour will have to ask him, and he produced -- and the result was these two documents. So perhaps we should ask where these -- whom he telephoned and what these two documents purport to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps may I suggest a different way? Couldn't we ask the witness what he knows about it, without using these documents, and then once they're translated we might see that this is reported in police reports and that we could perhaps use them as contextual exhibits or something like that, supporting what the witness said, and then we could go relatively quickly through it. Because I take it that -- I don't know yet what the relevance is, but if you, in questioning -- in examining the witness could make clear to us what -- because at the earlier occasion, the witness said, "I don't want to hide anything." Perhaps he doesn't want to hide anything here as well. But of course the Chamber might not be fully interested in all events that someone might ever think useful to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't want to waste any more time, but respectfully, I agree entirely with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's my fault for putting the document in front of him. I then thought immediately the best thing was to deal with it by narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Forget the documents for the moment, Mr. Milincic. Just tell the learned Judges what you know of this unfortunate incident, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: On this day, it was on the 11th or the 12th - I can't remember exactly - but at some point around 11.00 at night, I was informed, at home, by telephone, that the mosque at Kobas was on fire. And my reaction was, "So what did you do? Did you send the fire brigade in?" And they said "Yes, the fire brigade had gone to the mosque." There is a distance of about 20 kilometres between Srbac and Kobas. As to how fast the fire brigade was, well, when they got there, they did spray the mosque with water, but the roof had already caved in. I think we do have a report from the fire brigade. And judge went to do an on-the-spot check and there were some inspectors, and some technicians -- technical experts, rather. At any rate, the mosque was burnt down that night. The fire-fighters went there, but they did nothing much. They were unable to put the fire out soon enough. And now there is some speculation about this. Well, there was thunder, and there was a thunderstorm, and so the first version was that there was a lightning which caused the fire. It was a wooden mosque and now we've got a new, fancy one. And the second version was that it was set alight by the Serbs. And the third version was that it was set to light by the Muslims themselves, in -- because of the risk and danger, because there were Serb refugees travelling through Kobas. And those were refugees who were leaving their homes because of the war. And they were on their way to Serbia. And the locals were afraid that if those Serb refugees would see the mosque -- well, but this is just speculation, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You say it's speculation. The Chamber is not that interested in speculation. The Chamber noted, however, that you gave three options of speculation, two of them you just mentioned them, the third one got a lot of attention. Let's see, has there been ever established who was responsible for what was responsible for the fire at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an inquiry. I can see on the basis of these documents here that a judge was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what the result of that investigation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, because I've left Srbac, so I'm no longer involved in the political life there, but apparently the real reason was never established, the real reason for the mosque having been set alight. That's quite true. Go and ask any of the citizens and they will tell you the same. Nobody was brought to trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So what you tell us is the mosque caught fire, it was taken very seriously by the local authorities sending the firemen there, and that an investigation did not reveal what or who caused that fire. That's the basics of what you wanted to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I want to do in tab 13 is to submit those two documents that have today's fax date on. The others, as far as I'm concerned, can come out of the bundle and we can save the CLSS the trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll -- do you want to introduce them as contextual exhibits? Then there's no need to give them a number. At this moment, if you say they are contextual but perhaps already in the context of this testimony I'd like to tender it, then it will be given a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would like that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A number, Mr. Registrar, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse. Seven minutes left. I don't know whether you'll find a subject that you could deal with in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to deal now - we'll see if we can do it in seven minutes - with Mr. Krajisnik. When did you first meet Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: A difficult one. I saw him on television, when he was the Speaker of the Assembly, of the Joint Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then, when we met and how we met, I can't remember. It's all blurred in my memory. I suppose it was back in 1991 at some point, at the Holiday Inn. I think I met him at the Holiday Inn in 1991. I can't remember if it was in June or thereabouts. But it was a fleeting meeting. But I'm more familiar with him through his work as the Speaker of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The meeting that you went to at the Holiday Inn in 1991 was of which organisation or which body?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I think it was the SDS assembly, and the Main Board was being elected. And on that occasion, I was elected as member of that Main Board. And I think that Mr. Krajisnik became either a member of the party or of the Main Board. I can't remember. I'm not sure. Maybe he had already joined the party before and then he became a member of the Main Board on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You're digressing for one moment. How would you assess your memory, bearing in mind these events were 13 years ago or so, of events nationally or at the republic level of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: I do remember certain events. Others I probably don't remember. I mean, time goes by and certain things I thought were of no consequence, I and focussed more on problems affecting my own municipality, since there was a state of war, and I felt I should do all I could in order to save my own municipality. That was my main concern. I used to call it fate. It was a fateful decision to join politics. And all my activity really focussed on my municipality. But, of course, thank God, I do remember certain events and certain people. Time passes and erases certain memories. That's true, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When, if at all, did Mr. Krajisnik come to Srbac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 12th of October, we have a holiday in Srbac, our patron saint's day. And in 1994, after many problems and difficulties, we finally finished the post office building. It was a facility which meant a great deal to Srbac, and it was supposed to be opened, and I phoned -- or maybe I wrote -- I can't remember exactly whether I sent a letter setting out all the details, about a month in advance, and I basically booked the presence of Mr. Karadzic, the president of the Republic, and Mr. Krajisnik, the Srbac -- for the opening ceremony, and for them to visit Srbac at least once. And I was told that they would attend, that they would attend the opening ceremony. However, they didn't show up -- or rather, they were late. So they actually missed Srbac, and so they just went to a village near Srbac and had dinner there. After the ceremony, we had opened the post office and they joined us for dinner, and they spent a couple of hours with us and then they left to Banja Luka. And that was the first visit by Mr. Krajisnik in Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: From your dealings with Mr. Krajisnik, and indeed from your observing him on the television, what assessment did you make of his character?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MILINCIC
utterances.text: The same as now. Stable, witty, ready to compromise, and he was very skilful in acting as the Speaker of the Assembly. And those assembly meetings tended to be rather sensitive. What I mean is the Bosnia-Herzegovinian assembly. And he was pretty tactful and witty, and all the mutual jabs or all the possible tensions that were ready to flare up at any minute from the very start was something that Mr. Krajisnik knew how to keep under control in a certain way, and for that reason I suppose he must have had certain problems with Serbs as well, who probably would have liked him to take sides more clearly, to somehow root for the Serbs, as it were. But I believe that the SDS leadership gave him their support in his doing his best in order to make sure that the assembly was able to work and function properly. And he was quite popular amongst the population because of this style, in moderating sometimes difficult political discussions and topics, and very often mediating conclusions and decisions, et cetera. I believe that he used to do his best, really, in order for this assembly to continue to exist and not be dissolved. And unfortunately one day it was dissolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm going to pause there, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day, Mr. Milincic. I'd like to see you back tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00, not in this same courtroom. I'm afraid that I informed you yesterday wrongly about the courtroom. Although the schedule says that we're sitting in Courtroom I, we are actually sitting in Courtroom II tomorrow in the afternoon. It has been changed. So we'd like to see you back at a quarter past 2.00. I'd like to instruct you that you should speak with -- to no one about the testimony you have given until now and the testimony you're still about to give tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I read it in all the papers that I was given, that that was the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, the estimate you gave before, is that still valid?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. I'm going to -- I chatted to Mr. Krajisnik at the last break. He and I have come to a practical arrangement as to how I can use my remaining time to suit both of us, and I'm confident that I will take no more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Tieger, I know it was your wish, due to the way you received the information, that you would not start any cross-examination today. That now has been automatically fulfilled. At the same time, I take it that, of course, unexpected circumstances apart, that you'll be able to start cross-examining the witness after half an hour? I'm not saying that you should -- that you could not reserve the rights, in view of documents that are not translated, and as we did before, the Prosecution was allowed to revisit certain matters which it could not possibly look at sufficiently before the start of the cross-examination, but apart from that point, could you start cross-examination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Excuse me. Thank you. I understand, and that's my expectation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Then we'll adjourn, and I would like to thank the interpreters and the technicians for the four and a half minutes I've stolen from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour's reminded me. I, too, actually wanted to thank them, because I know how difficult it is for them when these documents have not been translated, and on behalf of the Defence, I really need to thank them very much for their understanding in our difficult circumstances. Your Honour has reminded me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
